what: Legence provides engineering and services that make buildings use less energy. It designs and installs mechanical, heating and cooling systems, commissions and optimises them, and maintains them afterwards — increasingly for data centres, semiconductor plants, hospitals and laboratories where the systems are complex and failure is costly.
customers: Owners and developers of technically demanding buildings: data centre operators, semiconductor and pharmaceutical manufacturers, hospitals, universities and large commercial landlords.
money: Design and installation of mechanical and energy systems in new and retrofitted buildings.
Commissioning, optimisation and ongoing maintenance contracts.
moat: Buildings that must hold precise temperature and air quality — a chip fabrication plant, a data centre, an operating theatre — need engineers who have done it before, and the pool of firms that can is small. Maintenance contracts that follow installation produce recurring revenue, and the engineer who built the system is the natural choice to maintain it.
risks: Reported net income of $45.1M against $4.3B of revenue, with a price/earnings ratio of 90.0 and 21.3 times EV/EBITDA, means the valuation rests on future earnings rather than current ones.
Seventeen analysts average a $72.18 target against a $35.09 price, a 106% gap that signals extraordinary disagreement about the company’s prospects.
The company listed recently and has a short public record, with revenue history available only from 2023.
Debt of $960.8M against $230.2M of cash reflects the private equity ownership that preceded the listing.
Data centre construction is the main growth driver and it is a concentrated, cyclical source of demand.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $1.6B in 2023 to $2.6B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $4.3B.
Free cash flow of $298.3M on $4.3B of revenue is strong for an engineering services business.
Data centre and semiconductor plant construction need exactly this capability, and both are in sustained expansion.
Maintenance contracts following installation produce recurring revenue at better margins than the construction work.
Energy efficiency retrofits are driven by regulation and operating cost rather than by discretionary spending.
watch: Backlog and the services share of revenue. Installation work is lumpy and project-based; the maintenance and services layer is what makes this a business rather than a contractor.
view: Legence sits in the middle of two of the strongest construction demand trends there are: data centres and semiconductor plants. Both are buildings where the mechanical systems are the hard part — a chip fabrication plant needs air cleanliness and temperature stability that ordinary construction cannot deliver, and a data centre is essentially a cooling problem with computers inside. The pool of engineering firms that can do this work competently is small, and that scarcity is the business.

The growth reflects it. Revenue went from $1.6 billion in 2023 to $2.6 billion in 2025 and $4.3 billion trailing, with $298 million of free cash flow. For an engineering services business that converts well. The more interesting part of the model is the services layer: the firm that designed and installed a complex mechanical system is the natural choice to commission, optimise and maintain it, and maintenance contracts carry better margins than installation and recur.

What makes the stock difficult is the combination of a short public record and a very high multiple. The company listed recently, revenue history is available only from 2023, and it carries $961 million of debt from its private equity ownership. Reported net income of $45 million on $4.3 billion of revenue puts the price/earnings ratio at 90 and EV/EBITDA at 21.3. Neither of those is a price you pay for a construction services firm; they are prices you pay for an infrastructure growth story.

The seventeen analysts averaging $72.18 against a $35.09 share price is the widest disagreement I have seen on a company this size, and it tells you something real: nobody knows how to model this yet. Engineering contractors are historically cyclical and historically prone to project losses, and the current demand is concentrated in data centre construction — which is strong, and which has a cycle. Backlog and the services share of revenue are the two figures that would distinguish a durable business from a boom-time contractor, and I would want several years of both before paying this multiple.
bull: Data centre and semiconductor construction keeps growing while the recurring maintenance layer expands, turning a scarce engineering capability into a durable services franchise.
bear: Data centre construction cools, project losses appear as they historically do in contracting, and a 90 times earnings multiple on a short record collapses.
